newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Murdoch's NZ publisher sees higher profits.
newsitem.headline: Murdoch's NZ publisher sees higher profits.

text.p: New Zealand publisher Independent Newspapers Ltd, controlled by media baron Rupert Murdoch, reported a higher annual profit on Friday and expects further gains in 1998 despite a slow economy.
INL, publisher of many of the country's major daily newspapers and considered a bellwether stock, said advertising volumes had been hit at the start of the 1998 year by the weakening economy.
But managing director Mike Robson told Reuters he still expected the group to better its 1996/97 net profit of NZ$50.4 million ($32.3 million), up from last year's $47.2 million.
"We think we'll be better than the $50 million," he said.
Roger Armstrong, share analyst at Doyle Paterson Brown, said INL's 1997 result was slightly better than expectations and the company looked well placed to improve earnings.
"There was just a firmer tone to all operations than we would have expected. It's an extremely good result in this economy," he said.

"The last quarter has just been horrifically bad and these guys have been hit by that. Their advertising volumes are down quite savagely in the last quarter. If it wasn't for that, they would have had a beauty result."
Robson said the company's net profit will improve in 1998 partly because abnormal writedowns had depressed the latest result.

INL has restructured the Australian operations of Gordon and Gotch. Robson said the magazine distributor had made a greatly improved contribution in the second half and would continue to make gains in the new financial year.
Analysts are forecasting a net profit for INL of about $63 million for the 1998 year, but that is before details of the company's expected purchase of a stake in Sky Network Television are known.
Robson had little to say about INL's plan to buy into the loss-making New Zealand pay-TV operator, which is not related to Murdoch's satellite Sky firms.
INL is currently in negotiations to buy the 51 percent of Sky held by HKP Partners, a U.S. consortium owned by Bell Atlantic, Ameritech, TCI Communications and Time Warner.

It is INL's second attempt at securing a piece of Sky after protracted talks broke down in February this year. Robson said he was not concerned that the company's negotiations with HKP Partners were also proving to be a drawn out affair.
"We're in negotiations and we're reasonably satisfied, but we'll make an announcement on that when we've completed them," he said, adding he expected a resolution "shortly".

He said once the Sky deal had been sewn up, INL may look to divest its U.S. assets, which include newspapers in Houston and in California. Analysts estimate the U.S. assets could fetch in the region of NZ$40 million.
INL's share price closed unchanged on Friday at NZ$7.90. (US$=1.56NZ$)
